title: Rage Against the Machines: From the Luddites to the AI Data Center Backlash
description:
in History, Technology |   	September 18th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One often-repeat­ed anec­dote about Mil­ton Fried­man has the famous eco
body:
in History, Technology |   	September 18th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One often-repeat­ed anec­dote about Mil­ton Fried­man has the famous econ­o­mist vis­it­ing a canal under con­struc­tion in nine­teen-six­ties Chi­na. Notic­ing the sheer num­ber of human labor­ers dig­ging away with shov­els, he asked the offi­cial in charge why they weren’t get­ting the work done faster with exca­va­tors and oth­er mod­ern machines. The bureau­crat explained to him that doing it by hand cre­at­ed more jobs. Fried­man’s reply: “If it’s jobs you want, you should give those men spoons instead.” Whether or not this exchange ever actu­al­ly hap­pened, it illus­trates a con­flict that’s arisen more than once in the his­to­ry of civ­i­liza­tion, pos­si­bly since the dawn of indus­tri­al­iza­tion — and at least since the hey­day of the Lud­dites.
Accord­ing to the Uni­ver­si­ty of Cam­bridge, that hey­day came in 1812, the year of “an assault by some 150 armed labor­ers on a Hud­der­s­field mill, in which sol­diers opened fire on the mob to stop them break­ing into the premis­es, fatal­ly wound­ing two attack­ers.” This was the cul­mi­na­tion of a series of protests across Eng­land, all of them inspired by anger at “new tech­nolo­gies, like auto­mat­ed looms, which were being used in the tex­tile indus­try in place of the skilled work of arti­sans, threat­en­ing their liveli­hoods as a result.” These des­per­ate­ly infu­ri­at­ed pro­test­ers, whose doc­u­ment­ed actions include the mur­der of a York­shire mill own­er, loud­ly expressed alle­giance to one Ned Ludd, a weaver said to have tak­en the bold step of smash­ing a cou­ple of new­fan­gled stock­ing frames some 25 years before.
The sto­ry of Lud­d’s ear­ly stand against mech­a­niza­tion may be even more ques­tion­able than the one about Mil­ton Fried­man and the spoons, but his name sur­vives today nev­er­the­less. In fact, it’s under­gone some­what of a revival thanks to the arti­fi­cial-intel­li­gence boom of recent years, dur­ing which even the mod­ern “knowl­edge work­ers” have come to fear the tram­pling of their liveli­hoods under tech­nol­o­gy’s inex­orable march. Their calls for restric­tions on the devel­op­ment and deploy­ment of AI are, in one side’s fram­ing of the argu­ment, mere­ly the lat­est pub­lic spasm of Lud­dism, a move­ment explained in the video above from The His­to­ry Guy. How many here in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry, after all, would argue that the mass pro­duc­tion of socks ulti­mate­ly con­sti­tut­ed a real loss for human­i­ty?
Lud­dism nev­er did count a large pro­por­tion of the Eng­lish labor force as its own. Rather, the move­ment appealed to “a rel­a­tive­ly ‘elite’ group” of legal­ly pro­tect­ed work­ers only allowed into their pro­fes­sions after years of appren­tice­ship, at which point “they tend­ed to feel that they were owed a liv­ing.” Nor did the con­di­tions, hours, and com­pen­sa­tion at the fac­to­ries then spring­ing up seem favor­able com­pared to the way of life enjoyed by their pre­de­ces­sors. Sim­i­lar sen­ti­ments may under­lie the “Lud­dite clubs” form­ing on col­lege cam­pus­es, on which NPR has report­ed, or this year’s social media-free “Sum­mer of Ludd” at the New School, to say noth­ing of ongo­ing protests against data-cen­ter con­struc­tion. It would be fas­ci­nat­ing to hear what gen­uine nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry Lud­dites would make of our sit­u­a­tion. Per­haps, one day, we can use AI to res­ur­rect them.

body:
in Art, History |   	September 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

With the Bayeux Tapes­try now on dis­play at the British Muse­um, Deep Down His­to­ry presents a deep dive into the embroi­dery’s full sto­ry:
“The Bayeux Tapes­try is one of the most remark­able sur­vivals of the Mid­dle Ages — a 70 metre embroi­dered account of the events lead­ing to the Nor­man Con­quest of Eng­land in 1066, cul­mi­nat­ing in the Bat­tle of Hast­ings. This video tells the Tapes­try’s sto­ry in full, using Charles Stothard’s ear­ly colour repro­duc­tion, pre­sent­ed here as a seam­less scroll for the first time. We fol­low Harold God­win­son’s fate­ful jour­ney from Edward the Con­fes­sor’s court to Nor­mandy, his lat­er seizure of the Crown, and William the Con­queror’s inva­sion. Beyond its polit­i­cal mes­sag­ing, the Tapes­try is also burst­ing with medieval his­to­ry, includ­ing jokes, fas­ci­nat­ing tech­ni­cal details, and a warn­ing for those who break their promis­es…”
Enjoy!

title: The Genius Logic of the NATO Phonetic Alphabet: How It Was Created & How It Works
description:
in History, Language |   	September 16th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Most of us can rat­tle off the first few words-that-stand-for-let­ters of
body:
in History, Language |   	September 16th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Most of us can rat­tle off the first few words-that-stand-for-let­ters of the NATO pho­net­ic alpha­bet. Alfa, Bra­vo, and Char­lie no doubt come right to mind, and depend­ing on how many war movies you’ve seen, so may Delta, Echo, and Fox­trot. But how many of us would rec­og­nize Kilo, Mike, and Sier­ra? For that mat­ter, how much do any of us know about how these par­tic­u­lar words came to be used to spell out oth­er words when com­mu­ni­cat­ing over walkie-talkies or oth­er low-fideli­ty com­mu­ni­ca­tion sys­tems? In the video above for his YouTube chan­nel Rob­Words, YouTu­ber Rob Watts explains the devel­op­ment of and log­ic behind the NATO pho­net­ic alpha­bet, wast­ing no time in clar­i­fy­ing that it isn’t a pho­net­ic alpha­bet, nor was it cre­at­ed by NATO.
What we actu­al­ly have here, Watts says, is a “spelling alpha­bet,” and its sto­ry goes back to the inven­tion of the tele­phone in the eigh­teen-sev­en­ties. “Ear­ly tele­phon­ists found that if ever they need­ed to spell some­thing out, like some­one’s name, one let­ter would get mis­heard as anoth­er.” The idea of express­ing each let­ter with a com­mon word start­ing with that let­ter arose nat­u­ral­ly, though fig­ur­ing out exact­ly which words to use took a lot more tri­al and error.
In the ear­ly nine­teen-tens, West­ern Union pub­lished a spelling alpha­bet con­sist­ing most­ly of the names of peo­ple and places: Adams, Boston, Chica­go, Den­ver, Edward, and so on. By World War I, the British army had also imple­ment­ed a rather more eccen­tric ver­sion, using words like Beer, Mon­key, Nuts, Orange, Pip, and York­er; by World War II, “every armed ser­vice in Britain and the U.S. had devel­oped its own spelling alpha­bet.”
In light of the rapid­ly glob­al­iz­ing nature of human affairs, and not just the mil­i­tary kind, the need for a sin­gle uni­ver­sal spelling alpha­bet became press­ing. It was­n’t until the estab­lish­ment of the Inter­na­tion­al Civ­il Avi­a­tion Orga­ni­za­tion, meant to over­see the skies in peace­time, that earnest work began on a revi­sion of the U.S.-U.K. com­bined forces’ exist­ing spelling alpha­bet, incor­po­rat­ing Eng­lish words eas­i­ly pro­nounce­able by non-Eng­lish speak­ers, while also being min­i­mal­ly con­fus­able for one anoth­er. By 1956, ICAO final­ized its list, which has remained the NATO pho­net­ic alpha­bet (or, offi­cial­ly, the Inter­na­tion­al Radiotele­pho­ny Spelling Alpha­bet) we all know today — or we at least par­tial­ly know. It may well be worth your time to mem­o­rize the rest, since you nev­er know when you’ll have to keep your Papas and Que­becs straight.

title: How Reading Changes the Way Your Brain Works
description:
in Books, Psychology |   	September 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Read­ing is unnat­ur­al. This will hard­ly come as a sur­prise to any chil
body:
in Books, Psychology |   	September 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Read­ing is unnat­ur­al. This will hard­ly come as a sur­prise to any child try­ing to put off his home­work for just one more hour of watch­ing oth­er kids play Minecraft. Yet there real­ly are impli­ca­tions worth con­sid­er­ing if we accept that our cog­ni­tive sys­tems did­n’t evolve to process text in the same way as they evolved to han­dle vision and speech. Speak­ing on an evo­lu­tion­ary his­tor­i­cal scale, “we haven’t had enough time to devel­op a ded­i­cat­ed read­ing brain,” says UCLA neu­ro­sci­en­tist Rebec­ca Gotlieb in the BBC World Ser­vice video above. For the time being, in a kind of cog­ni­tive jer­ry-rig­ging, “we co-opt parts of the brain involved in vision and audi­to­ry pro­cess­ing and lan­guage and atten­tion and affect.”
That was true for read­ers and writ­ers of Sumer­ian cuneiform and Egypt­ian hiero­glyph­ics five mil­len­nia ago. It still is for read­ers and writ­ers of the many scripts in use today, from the Latin alpha­bet to Chi­nese char­ac­ters to the Ara­bic abjad, each of which has its own influ­ence on its users’ neu­ro­log­i­cal archi­tec­ture. One of the biggest dif­fer­ences between then and now is the scale of read­ing: ancient Sume­ria and Egypt seem to have had lit­er­a­cy rates around one per­cent, a num­ber com­pris­ing most­ly scribes, priests, and nobles, while the glob­al aver­age today comes in around 88 per­cent and ris­ing. Anoth­er is the medi­um of read­ing: the shift from papyrus to paper may have seemed remark­able at the time, but the more recent one from paper to elec­tron­ic screens has already changed the way we think about our world.
“When we read on screens, we tend to skim, and when we skim, we’re more sus­cep­ti­ble to mis­in­for­ma­tion,” says Gotlieb. So we’ve been told, many times and many ways, amid the past decade’s ever-more-trou­bled polit­i­cal reportage. In 2018, Maryanne Wolf, author of Come Home: The Read­ing Brain in a Dig­i­tal World, argued in the Guardian that the “sub­tle atro­phy of crit­i­cal analy­sis and empa­thy” appar­ent­ly caused by tech­nol­o­gy-encour­aged skim­ming “affects our abil­i­ty to nav­i­gate a con­stant bom­bard­ment of infor­ma­tion. It incen­tivizes a retreat to the most famil­iar silos of unchecked infor­ma­tion, which require and receive no analy­sis, leav­ing us sus­cep­ti­ble to false infor­ma­tion and dem­a­goguery.”
So much for us adults. What about the chil­dren? In the BBC World Ser­vice video, Wolf blunt­ly sums up the results of stud­ies so far on the effects of ear­ly read­ing expe­ri­ence on lat­er intel­lec­tu­al per­for­mance: “the more dig­i­tal, the worse aca­d­e­m­ic.” If a young brain is “con­stant­ly being dis­tract­ed and hyper­stim­u­lat­ed, you’re going to have them not able to real­ly move from one stim­u­lus to the next with­out a desire for ever-quick­er inter­vals between stim­uli.” For our part, as par­ents, teach­ers, or oth­er vis­i­ble exam­ples of grown-uphood, we can do noth­ing to coun­ter­act that more effec­tive­ly than to mod­el and enjoy a rich “read­ing life” for the next gen­er­a­tion. We must, in oth­er words, pick up books and not put them down, which may strike an Open Cul­ture read­er as an easy task. But ask your­self this: how many times did you click over to some­thing else before get­ting to the end of this post?

title: The Largest Roman Mosaic Ever Excavated Opens to the Public
description: At 33 feet wide and 52.5 feet high, an ancient mosaic recently unveiled to the public may be the largest in the entire Roman world. It sits within
body:
At 33 feet wide and 52.5 feet high, an ancient mosaic recently unveiled to the public may be the largest in the entire Roman world. It sits within the recently opened Museum of the Baths of Trajan in central Rome, which preserves a monumental, early 2nd-century bath complex built by Emperor Trajan covering about 15 acres.
To construct the baths on the Oppian Hill, builders repurposed elements of a previous structure, Emperor Nero’s Domus Aurea, or “Golden House,” originally erected between 64 and 68 C.E. It’s unclear if the mosaic originated in that building; archaeologists think it could have also been part of a lavish dwelling that was later incorporated into the compound. But many of the monumental composition’s tesserae are missing and may have been used in the construction of the baths.

Dubbed the “Great Mosaic,” the work was discovered in 2011, and archaeologists have been meticulously revealing and conserving it since. The in situ artwork depicts architectural features that may represent a dual-level theatrical set, known as a scaenae frons, plus statues of the Muses and other figures and patterns that mimic the appearance of marble.
Within the same complex, a remarkable architectural fresco uncovered in the 1990s also goes on view for the first time. Known as the “Painted City,” it’s unclear whether the scenic backdrop for bathers depicts an actual port city or an imaginary place. According to CNN, the aerial perspective portrays some unusual details such as public squares and towers that weren’t a common feature of municipal design in the 1st century.
Archaeologists continue to excavate the “Great Mosaic,” particularly an area focusing on wine-making and grapes. Much of it can now be seen by visitors from an elevated walkway.

title: Art by Humans, For Humans: A Letter from Our Editorial Director
description:
Dear Reader,
The New York Times recently asked dozens of 10-year-olds what the world will be like in 2050. Some are hopeful: a woman will finally
body:
Dear Reader,
The New York Times recently asked dozens of 10-year-olds what the world will be like in 2050. Some are hopeful: a woman will finally be president of the U.S., people will be more kind, and everyone will have a pet fox. Others, though, feel as if they’ve been plucked straight from a dystopian hellscape: world wars, monarchic rule supplanting voting, embedded brain sensors that send your thoughts straight to an app, and the end of human civilization entirely. Whether optimistic or not, these children mention A.I. again and again. In their futures, it’s an inextricable fixture of life.
A.I.’s exponential growth has accelerated fears about its power, prompting numerous executives and technologists to warn that it’s time to slow such rapid expansions. Whatever your feelings, it’s clear that we’re collectively witnessing a moment that will shape our world for generations.
For artists, illustrators, designers, and writers like me, A.I. is not only a threat to our livelihoods but to the very substance of our humanity. The question is not whether a bot could create a technically proficient painting or describe a sculpture with more insight than I could, but rather about what we lose from outsourcing the singular technology that is ours. Art is uniquely human and one of the greatest drivers of empathy and connection with one another. As I’ve come to understand, it’s also a true act of faith in a world that can make hope feel impossible.
For the past seven years, I’ve spoken with thousands of curious and creative people striving each day to draw attention to the misunderstood, the overlooked, and the unimaginable. Artists are uniquely primed to envision alternative ways of being, and in their profound acts of generosity, they share their hopes for the great and small with us. Their faith, in turn, becomes something we can all take part in.
Colossal operates on generosity, too, propelled not by an algorithm or an A.I. model but by a devoted team of just four people. We strive to ensure that the widest array of readers, from students and educators to fellow creatives and art appreciators, have the opportunity to engage with artists’ work they might not otherwise encounter. We also prioritize a deeply human process. Every facet of the magazine, from selecting images to writing headlines to compiling our daily newsletter, is done with our hands. 
Although we certainly could be more efficient if we automated and outsourced our efforts, we know that would be the end of what makes Colossal what it is. We understand that in embracing friction, we’re supporting the artists, illustrators, designers, and more who have so generously shared themselves and their dreams with us. We’re also actively creating the world we want to live in.
But we can’t do this alone. An intentional and people-powered process like ours requires real resources, and less than 0.5% of our weekly readership financially contributes to Colossal. Increasing that support to 1% would mean cementing our long-term survival and ensuring we can continue to celebrate the unbridled human creativity that has come to characterize the magazine for the last 16 years.
Becoming a Colossal Member is both an act of generosity and a direct line to the work that matters. Colossal Members believe in the power of creativity and have faith that it can help usher in a better tomorrow. When there’s a rapid shift to sleek, frictionless life, they champion the nuanced, messy, and idiosyncratic, and the art that can only be made by humans, for humans.
Yours in hope,Grace EbertEditorial director, Colossal

title: Pablo Luna Studio Takes Inspiration from Nature for Its Climate-Responsive Architecture
description: Inspired by shapes and movement found in nature, Pablo Luna Studio conceives of hospitality spaces, wellness retreats, and homes that sympathize w
body:
Inspired by shapes and movement found in nature, Pablo Luna Studio conceives of hospitality spaces, wellness retreats, and homes that sympathize with their surroundings. Rather than creating a barrier between outside and inside, the airy structures welcome foliage and the natural landscape into the overall experience, blurring the boundary between structure and environment.
The firm, based in Ubud, Bali, Indonesia, is dedicated to building with nature, incorporating sustainable materials and taking a climate-responsive approach. “Imagine a home that stays cool in summer without constant air conditioning, or warm in winter with minimal heating, simply by virtue of its design,” the studio says. “This isn’t magic; it’s the intelligent application of climate responsive architecture. It’s about leveraging natural forces like sun, wind, and rain, transforming them from challenges into design opportunities.”
Lotus Yoga Shala
Recent projects include the Lotus Shala in Ubud, which takes the lotus—a symbol of purity and awakening—as inspiration for an elegantly concave wooden canopy with open sides supported by posts, so that those inside feel connected to their tropical surroundings. It’s built entirely from bamboo, which is an incredibly strong yet flexible material, allowing the team to create graceful curves complemented by geometric precision.
In Sanskrit, “shala” means “home,” and the spiritual practice of yoga is complemented by purpose-built pavilion designs that encourage harmony and calm. Pablo Luna Studio’s Manta Shala is yet another example, perched on the coastline of Nusa Penida, Indonesia, with an undulating roofline that evokes the way a manta ray’s body creates a gentle, wave-like motion as it swims.
Additional projects include an eco-lodge in Uganda and numerous villas, restaurants, and wellness destinations in Bali. See more on the studio’s Instagram.
